target.title: fix(agents): preserve ANSI sanitizer state across bash chunks
target.body:
Closes #103668

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running bash commands through agents could see ANSI/OSC control-sequence fragments leak into streamed tool output, final bash results, and full-output spill files when a process split a terminal sequence across output callbacks.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adds a reusable incremental ANSI sequence stripper in terminal-core and lets the bash output accumulator use one sanitizer instance for the lifetime of each command. This preserves streaming and bounded-memory behavior while keeping one-shot `stripAnsiSequences()` semantics unchanged for existing callers.

## User Impact

Bash output sanitization is now invariant to callback chunking for OSC and CSI sequences. Agents and users receive the same clean output whether the process emits a complete sequence in one callback or splits it across callbacks.

## Evidence

Before this patch, sanitizing `A\x1b]0;title` and `\x07B` independently leaked fragments such as `Aitle\x07B`; whole-input sanitization returned `AB`.

target.title: feat(fleet): harden create, port allocation, drift visibility, and operator docs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Operational rough edges in the experimental fleet supervisor, collected from review and live testing of #104527/#104669: create reported success on broken images, image drift under mutable tags was invisible, host port collisions surfaced as opaque container errors, `openclaw security audit` guidance predated the multi-tenant docs, and backup/platform expectations were undocumented. Closes #104791.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Health-gated create.** `create` now uses the same bounded `/healthz` wait as `upgrade` (extracted into one shared `waitForHealthyCell` helper with a closed result union — no duplicated loop). Failure semantics deliberately differ and are commented: upgrade restores the previous container; create has none, so an unhealthy new cell is *kept* (container + registry row) as diagnosable evidence, and the error points at `fleet status|logs|rm`. `--no-start` skips the gate. Docs note that the token of an unhealthy new cell remains recoverable from the container env, and rm+recreate is always safe pre-traffic.
- **Image drift visibility.** `fleet status` now surfaces the live image ID from inspection (no schema change), so a cell left behind by a moving `latest` is visible; digest pinning via `--image ...@sha256:...` is verified by test and documented.
- **Port bind probing.** Before reserving, create probe-binds `127.0.0.1:<candidate>`: an explicit `--port` in host use fails with a clear error; auto-allocation skips host-busy ports and retries reservation races (registry transaction still arbitrates concurrent creates; the deliberate TOCTOU acceptance is commented — the runtime bind stays authoritative).
- **Audit alignment.** The security audit's multi-user and attack-surface trust-model strings now point at the supported model: one isolated Gateway cell per tenant (docs link), matching what the product ships.
- **Docs.** Cold backup/restore recipe (both directories required — the auth-secrets dir holds the credential encryption keys; back up stopped, SQLite is not crash-consistent live; restore into a `--no-start` cell) and an explicit platform statement (Linux/macOS tested, Windows untested).

No new config keys, no new dependencies, no schema changes.

## User Impact

Broken images fail loudly at create instead of leaving silently dead cells; port conflicts fail early with a clear message; drift is visible in `status`; audit guidance matches the product; operators get a real backup story. Fleet remains experimental.

## Evidence

- Focused tests green on Blacksmith Testbox (fleet 130 + CLI + audit expectations; new coverage: healthy/never-healthy/`--no-start` create gating with evidence retention asserted, explicit-busy and auto-skip port probing incl. reservation races, digest ref pass-through, status image ID, audit strings): https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29173521401 (147 fleet/CLI tests + audit expectations, 3 shards green)
- `pnpm tsgo`, `pnpm check:test-types`, oxlint, `docs:map:check`: clean.
- Pre-existing failures explicitly ruled out: `src/security/audit-plugin-readonly-scope.test.ts` and `src/security/secret-equal.test.ts` fail identically on clean `origin/main` (verified by stash A/B) — unrelated to this diff.
- Structured autoreview (Codex): two build-phase findings accepted and fixed (concurrent port reservation retry, restore-options documentation); one finding resolved via docs (token recovery guidance) rather than new product surface. Final review: clean, "no accepted/actionable findings" (0.91), after a second cycle fixed two real probe-preflight findings: EACCES on privileged ports no longer rejects configs a rootful daemon can serve (probe fails open; runtime bind stays authoritative), and auto-allocation scans the full range instead of capping at 25 attempts (regression-tested).

target.title: fix(realtime): add timeout to WebRTC offer requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users starting a realtime WebRTC voice session could remain stuck waiting when the SDP offer request returned headers but the answer body stalled.

## Why This Change Was Made

The WebRTC offer fetch now uses an explicit 30s AbortController deadline that stays active until the SDP answer body has been read. The change keeps the existing setup cancellation and failure flow intact and limits the timeout to the WebRTC offer exchange.

## User Impact

Realtime voice setup now fails through the existing error state instead of spinning indefinitely when the offer response body stops progressing.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check` passed.
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local --engine claude` passed with no accepted/actionable findings.

This is not live OpenAI proof, but it exercises the browser fetch/body-read/AbortSignal path and the `chat-realtime` state machine that drives the visible UI status.

target.title: fix(msteams): reset sessions on app removal lifecycle
target.body:
Closes #99054

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams users who remove a personal app/bot and later add it again can continue the same OpenClaw server-side DM session, allowing the bot to use prior conversation context after an app lifecycle boundary.

This targets Teams app-management lifecycle signals that the bot can actually observe. Live capture showed Teams' local "Remove chat history" action can arrive later as an ordinary message in the same personal `conversation.id`, with no `installationUpdate`, `conversationUpdate`, `membersAdded`, or `membersRemoved` activity. This PR does not claim to detect that fully local clear-chat action when Teams gives the bot no lifecycle or conversation-boundary signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

Teams now routes `installationUpdate` removal activities and bot `membersRemoved` conversation updates into a lifecycle handler. On a removal boundary, the handler removes the cached Teams conversation reference, rotates the matching OpenClaw session entry to a new session id with `updatedAt: 0`, and clears provider-owned route/delivery/origin metadata so the next inbound message cannot resume the removed chat transcript.

The handler also treats a personal `installationUpdate action=add` as a reinstall boundary only when an existing route-matched Teams DM session is already active. That catches tenants or flows where the re-add signal is visible but the prior remove signal was missed, without resetting first-time installs. Finally, inbound personal DMs check for a stored same-user/same-bot conversation reference with a different Teams `conversation.id`; when Teams exposes that boundary, OpenClaw removes the previous reference and rotates the DM session.

## User Impact

After a true Teams app removal and re-add, the next inbound message starts from a fresh OpenClaw session instead of silently resuming prior DM or channel context. Operators also avoid retaining a cached proactive-send reference for the removed Teams conversation.

For Teams clear-chat/reopen flows, the patch protects the observable case where Teams gives the bot a new personal conversation id. If Teams reuses the same server-side conversation id and sends no lifecycle event, there is no bot-visible signal in the captured payloads; that remains a Teams platform limitation rather than a claim made by this PR.

Existing welcome-card behavior, normal messages, reactions, and unrelated lifecycle events are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Live corrected Dale smoke:
  - Baseline before app removal used a synthetic marker.
  - Teams app removal emitted `installationUpdate action=remove`.
  - Handler logged `msteams lifecycle remove handled`, `reason=installation-remove`, `conversationType=personal`, `conversationRemoved=true`, `sessionsReset=1`.
  - The session entry rotated to a new redacted session id with `updatedAt: 0` and no Teams route/delivery/origin metadata.
  - After re-add, Teams showed the welcome card and the verification prompt used a fresh session; the bot did not recall the pre-removal marker.
- Live Teams `Remove chat history` follow-up after deploying this branch:
  - Sent a synthetic pre-clear marker.
  - Used Teams `Remove chat history`, opened the app/chat again, and sent a verification prompt.
  - No `installationUpdate add`, lifecycle/remove activity, or DM conversation-boundary handler log appeared.
  - The same OpenClaw session id remained active, and the bot could recall the pre-clear marker.
  - This confirms the PR should not claim to fix Teams local clear-history behavior when Teams sends no lifecycle event and reuses the same server-side conversation id.
- Added regression coverage for:
  - personal `installationUpdate/remove`
  - personal `installationUpdate/remove-upgrade`
  - first-install `installationUpdate/add` with no active session
  - personal `installationUpdate/add` when an existing session is active
  - ignored channel `installationUpdate/add`
  - channel bot `membersRemoved`
  - ignored non-bot `membersRemoved`
  - race-safe session rotation
  - personal DM conversation-id boundary rotation
  - no rotation for matching personal conversation ids
  - no rotation for different stored bot ids
- Added monitor-level coverage proving the Teams activity shim dispatches `installationUpdate` and `membersRemoved` activities to registered lifecycle handlers.
- Validation:
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.test.ts` - 11 tests passed.
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.authz.test.ts` - 18 tests passed.
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams` - 71 files passed, 1007 tests passed.
  - `pnpm run lint:extensions:bundled` - passed.
  - `pnpm format:check extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.ts` - passed.
  - `git diff --check` - passed.



---

Migration note: This PR replaces #100371 with the same published head commit, moved from `spinen/openclaw` to `jimmypuckett/openclaw` so OpenClaw maintainers and repository automation can update the contribution without transferring authorship. Prior review, proof, and CI history remain available on #100371.

target.title: feat(ui): editable file panel with CodeMirror and sessions.files.set hash-CAS writes
target.body:
Closes #104698

## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI file detail panel (from #100615) is read-only, and file paths in tool cards are dead text. Operators reviewing an agent's work cannot make a small correction to a file the agent just touched — a doc typo, a config value — without leaving the browser, which is impossible when the workspace lives on a remote gateway host ("Open in editor" cannot reach it).

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Gateway**: new `sessions.files.set` RPC (`operator.admin`) that overwrites one existing workspace file with compare-and-swap semantics on a sha256 content hash. `sessions.files.get` now returns that hash for strict-UTF-8 text files (the hash doubles as the editability signal — binary previews never get one, and `set` independently rejects non-text targets so replacement-character re-encoding can never corrupt a binary file). Writes go through the same fs-safe root as reads (realpathed root, symlink/hardlink rejection, path containment, 256 KB UTF-8 cap); no create/delete. The workspace-browser module explicitly deferred general writes to a "separately reviewed mutation contract" — this PR is that contract, following the `agents.files.set` admin-scope precedent. Protocol change is additive (no version bump).
- **UI**: the file panel now renders through CodeMirror 6 for both viewing and editing, replacing the hand-rolled highlight.js line renderer (one canonical path; the old HTML-splitting helpers are deleted). Existing affordances are preserved: line numbers, jump-to-line, in-file search, copy, Show in Files, open-in-external-editor. Edit mode (pencil, gated on `sessions.files.set` advertisement + `operator.admin`) adds dirty tracking, Cmd/Ctrl-S save, and a conflict banner with Reload / Overwrite when the file changed on disk since load. CodeMirror ships as a lazy Vite chunk (`file-editor-view` 46 kB + per-language chunks), loaded on first panel open.
- **Tool cards**: file paths in expanded read/edit/write cards are now clickable and open the same panel (collapsed rows are untouched — they are already one big toggle button).
- One real bug found during live verification and fixed here: the app shell is slotted through the tooltip provider's shadow root, so CodeMirror's default root detection mounted its base theme into that shadow root where slotted light-DOM content can't see it. The editor now pins `root: document` (see the inline comment in `file-editor-view.ts`).

## User Impact

Operators with admin scope can view and edit workspace text files directly from chat context on any gateway, with agent-write conflict safety. Read-only operators and older gateways see the unchanged read-only viewer (the edit affordance is capability-gated). File references in tool cards become navigable like chat prose links already were.

## Evidence

Screenshots (mock gateway harness, `agent:alpha` fixture):

| Viewer | Edit mode (dirty) | Saved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![viewer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/file-editor-panel-104698/file-viewer.png) | ![dirty](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/file-editor-panel-104698/file-editor-dirty.png) | ![saved](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/file-editor-panel-104698/file-editor-saved.png) |

Validation:

- Gateway: `sessions-files` + `agents-workspace` suites green locally (both shards) and 40/40 on Blacksmith Testbox (Linux) for the initial RPC coverage. Cases: CAS happy path, stale-hash conflict with `currentHash`, missing file, >256 KB rejection, `../` escape + symlink containment (no write outside root), binary preview without a hash, binary write rejection even with a matching byte hash, UTF-8 BOM byte round-trip, and `set` skipping the transcript scan.
- UI: jsdom suites (`chat-sidebar`, `chat-tool-cards`) green; new Chromium browser suite (`chat-sidebar-file-view.browser.test.ts`) 7/7 covering render/target-line decoration, edit→dirty→save, CRLF round-trip through save, in-flight-save dirty tracking, conflict→Reload, edit-mode drop when a reload returns non-editable content, and read-only-while-reloading (skips cleanly in the jsdom shard, which also collects `*.browser.test.ts`).
- e2e: `chat-file-links.e2e.test.ts` green with no selector changes (the CodeMirror line decorations keep the `file-view__line--target`/`data-line` contract).
- Build: `vite build` green; CodeMirror in a separate lazy chunk (`file-editor-view-*.js` 46.25 kB gzip 13.25 kB; language definitions split per language).
- Live: full flow verified in the mock dev harness (open from workspace rail → CodeMirror view → edit → save), which now models `sessions.files.get` hashes and `sessions.files.set`.
- Autoreview (Codex, structured, iterated until clean): eight findings triaged — missing-lockfile was a bundle artifact (the real branch commits the lockfile; it was excluded from the review bundle because integrity hashes trip the secret scanner); the CAS-window finding is an accepted system bound (agents write from their own OS processes; documented inline); six were real and are fixed here with regression tests: binary/non-UTF-8 files could be "edited" and corrupted (no CAS hash for non-text now, `set` rejects non-text targets), UTF-8 BOMs were silently dropped on save (`ignoreBOM` decode), CRLF/CR files were normalized to LF on save (`EditorState.lineSeparator` + `sliceDoc` serialization), mixed-line-ending files now stay read-only (`hasUniformLineEndings` gate), a conflict Reload re-checks that gate and drops edit mode when the latest content no longer qualifies, and `set` rejects NUL-containing replacement content so the API never writes a file its own editability checks classify as binary.
- Known proof gaps: the local `npm shrinkwrap guard` lane fails in this environment on npm 12/Node 26 — it fails identically against `main`'s untouched lockfile, so it is environmental; hosted CI (Linux Node 24) is authoritative. Two Blacksmith Testbox leases died mid-`check:changed` (infra outage); all other local lanes were green.

target.title: fix(plugins): keep API key preview from splitting UTF-16 surrogate pairs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the API-key preview shown during provider setup could emit isolated UTF-16 surrogate halves when the pasted key contains astral characters (e.g., emoji).

## Why This Change Was Made

`formatApiKeyPreview` used raw `String.prototype.slice` for its head and tail snippets, which can cut through surrogate pairs. It now uses the repository's existing `sliceUtf16Safe` helper so the redacted preview always stays on valid UTF-16 boundaries. The change is limited to this display helper and its test.

## User Impact

Setup confirmation prompts and status output that display API-key previews remain well-formed when the key value contains non-BMP characters.

## Evidence

- Added regression tests in `src/plugins/provider-auth-input.test.ts` covering ASCII redaction and astral boundary cases.
- Existing provider auth input tests continue to pass.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Before the patch, `formatApiKeyPreview("a😀b")` returned `"a\ud83d…\ude00b"` (isolated surrogate halves at both edges). After the patch it returns `"a…b"`.
- **Real environment tested:** Local checkout of `fix/provider-auth-preview-utf16` at `32c627eb0a636e7efe694ebde1af27fb8edf95b8`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  node --import tsx -e 'import { formatApiKeyPreview } from "./src/plugins/provider-auth-input.ts"; for (const v of ["a😀b", "abc😀" + "x".repeat(20), "x".repeat(20) + "😀abc", "😀".repeat(10)]) console.log(JSON.stringify(formatApiKeyPreview(v)));'
  ```

target.title: fix(moonshot): resolve Kimi search secret refs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Kimi web search accepted `tools.web.search.kimi.apiKey` as a configured credential, but runtime lookup only handled string values before falling back to ambient `KIMI_API_KEY` / `MOONSHOT_API_KEY`.

That meant an env SecretRef configured at `tools.web.search.kimi.apiKey` was not resolved at runtime, and a missing configured ref could silently fall through to ambient env credentials.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Kimi web search provider now uses the shared web-search credential resolver for the configured apiKey path and preserves the existing env fallback list only when no configured credential is present.

The config type is widened so SecretRef objects can flow through the existing Kimi config plumbing instead of being treated as strings only.

## User Impact

Users can configure Kimi web search with an env SecretRef and have it resolve at runtime.

If the configured SecretRef is missing, Kimi search now fails closed instead of unexpectedly using ambient `KIMI_API_KEY` or `MOONSHOT_API_KEY`.

target.title: fix(browser): check own profile entries for profile operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Browser profile names are user-controlled config keys. Inherited object properties such as `constructor` and `prototype` were treated as real profile entries in several create, delete, projection, hot-reload, and gateway patch paths. A valid profile with one of those names could therefore be rejected, omitted, or fail to round-trip.

Live route testing also exposed an adjacent deletion failure: when `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` or `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` placed Browser state outside the OS home/temp roots, deleting a launched profile returned HTTP 500 because the trash helper rejected Browser's own configured state directory.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Use own-property checks at every Browser profile lookup boundary.
- Preserve valid top-level profile keys while continuing to strip nested prototype-pollution keys from untrusted config patches.
- Keep profile listing and hot reload consistent with persisted config.
- Authorize trash moves only from Browser's owned `<config>/browser` subtree. Existing realpath, symlink-escape, target-identity, and trash-destination checks remain in force; the wider config directory is not authorized.

## User Impact

Profiles named `constructor` or `prototype` can be created, listed, hot-reloaded, patched, and deleted normally. Custom state directories outside the home directory work without granting Browser deletion authority over unrelated config or filesystem paths.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `194d41eab680c1964c70087a60e03df607470878`
- Exact GitHub CI: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29032054298 - passed.

- Fresh autoreview at the exact head - clean, confidence 0.91.

target.title: fix(google-meet): guard node-host meet URLs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Google Meet chrome node-host command accepted any non-empty `start.url` before launching Chrome or starting realtime bridge processes. The higher-level node invoke policy already normalizes Meet URLs, but the node-host command is its own execution boundary and direct calls could still pass non-Meet URLs into local Chrome/bridge side effects.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the existing Google Meet URL contract into a lightweight shared helper and applies it inside `startChrome` before any BlackHole check, audio bridge startup, or Chrome launch. `runtime.ts` continues to re-export `normalizeMeetUrl`, while `node-invoke-policy.ts` imports the same helper directly so the policy and host boundary cannot drift.

## User Impact

Invalid or non-Meet URLs now fail fast with the same stable Google Meet URL errors used by the runtime and node invoke policy. Valid `https://meet.google.com/...` meeting URLs keep the same launch, bridge, list, and stop behavior.

## Evidence

- `extensions/google-meet/src/node-host.ts` now normalizes `params.url` with the shared Meet URL contract before local side effects.
- `extensions/google-meet/node-host.test.ts` covers a non-Meet realtime start request and proves neither `spawnSync` nor child processes are reached.
- `extensions/google-meet/src/runtime.ts` re-exports the helper so existing callers that import from runtime remain compatible.
- Direct node-host proof on current head invoked `handleGoogleMeetNodeHostCommand()` with `action=start`, `mode=realtime`, `launch=true`, and a non-Meet URL. It returned the Meet URL contract error on Linux before any bridge session existed or was created.

target.title: fix: stabilize embedded prompt caching across policy and Responses boundaries
target.body:
Related: #102175

## What Problem This Solves

Long-lived embedded sessions could lose prompt-cache reuse when the same session crossed room-event delivery, sender-policy, queue, compaction, recovery, or native Responses continuation boundaries.

The failure was not one cache knob. Turn-specific delivery and authorization changed reusable prompt/tool shape, reconstructed runs could drop authoritative state, and authenticated OpenAI Responses could miss native continuation.

## What Changed

- Keeps the model-visible prompt and ordered tool catalogue stable across owner, non-owner, trusted-internal, unknown-sender, and ambient room-event turns.
- Resolves one deterministic `ToolAccessPolicy` per turn and emits a trusted full snapshot only when permissions change or model state is uncertain.
- Denies unavailable `computer`, `cron`, `gateway`, and `nodes` calls with non-retryable `TOOL_ACCESS_DENIED` before hooks, implementations, or side effects.
- Carries immutable policy through loopback MCP grants; request headers cannot widen authority, and current-main capability/revocation checks remain intact.
- Keeps trusted-internal turns non-owner (`senderIsOwner: false`): policy can grant only the four protected core tools without exposing owner-only plugin tools.
- Separates actual reply delivery from the session-stable prompt-facing delivery mode, including `message_tool_only` room events.
- Propagates policy, owner identity, delivery modes, and forced snapshots through direct, queued, memory, preflight, manual, timeout, overflow, and after-turn compaction paths.
- Acknowledges policy persistence at provider-native durable boundaries for OpenClaw, Codex, and Copilot, with generation checks preventing stale acknowledgements from clearing newer state.
- Preserves native Codex supervision settings while appending trusted turn guidance as a developer history item before the user turn; no model, effort, personality, or collaboration-mode override is introduced.
- Routes built-in authenticated GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Responses streams through native `previous_response_id` continuation with delta input. Custom streams keep their existing routing.

The earlier experimental post-history developer-message split is not included; that request shape produced HTTP 400 responses on ChatGPT/Codex Responses. Native continuation is fixed through stream classification instead.

## Security And Compatibility

- Tool visibility is not authority. Every protected call is checked again against the immutable current-turn policy immediately before execution.
- Runtime-owned `cron`, `heartbeat`, and `memory` turns are distinct from unknown and explicit non-owner senders. Ambient room-event policy remains fail-closed.
- The model-facing tool-name hash omits turn-specific owner state; the runtime grant retains the effective decision.
- No persistent storage schema or migration is introduced.
- No private sender, channel, account, host, endpoint, credential, or raw trace identifiers are included.

## Evidence

The original same-session reproduction showed the model-visible inventory flipping between 44 and 47 tools, matching prompt/tool digest changes, and cached prefixes collapsing to roughly 2k-10k tokens or ceilinging around 37k-40k.

Numeric-only usage records from a long-lived room session after the stable-shape change show the cached prefix growing from 104,960 to 157,184 tokens. Its final four consecutive provider turns reported `cacheRead` 155,136 / 155,136 / 156,160 / 157,184 with uncached input 1,193 / 1,836 / 2,097 / 1,324, or 98.7-99.2% prefix reuse. Message text, sender/channel/session IDs, hosts, and credentials were excluded.

The exact candidate head was then exercised through isolated, non-delivered live-provider sessions:

- GPT-5.5: cold `input=41,110 cacheRead=0`; warm turns `input=188 cacheRead=40,960` and `input=226 cacheRead=40,960` (99.5% reuse).
- GPT-5.6 Sol: cold `input=41,108 cacheRead=0`; warm turns `input=698 cacheRead=40,448` and `input=736 cacheRead=40,448` (98.2-98.3% reuse).
- The system-prompt hash stayed constant within each model, the ordered catalogue remained 48 tools, and the aggregate ordered tool name/summary/schema digest was identical across warm turns and both models: `a66a993fb1099d80fd84f809b1d3ae408a7ed206d7b7598680c1563ae1d24a65`.

An exact-head focused proof run selected 14 assertions across 18 project suites with zero failures. It verifies room events remain contextual and `message_tool_only`, unauthorized non-owner and ambient calls return non-retryable `TOOL_ACCESS_DENIED` before hooks or implementation, trusted-internal calls execute, and GPT-5.5/GPT-5.6 send `previous_response_id` with delta-only input across unchanged and changed policy snapshots.

The exact candidate head is now built and running on the reporter's local gateway. The LaunchAgent uses the repo-local `dist/index.js`, runtime and RPC probes are healthy, the loopback dashboard returns HTTP 200, and `dist/build-info.json` reports the exact commit below.

## Exact-Head Validation

Candidate: `b0a9bfc589f8deff1ed9dd5345276093d6df25b2`

Upstream included in branch and used for merge-tree proof: `7027d2c227281d814266311bebab7581b899d6dc`

- merge-tree check against the latest fetched upstream is clean;
- pre-refresh broad validation passed 2,446 changed-file tests across unit-fast, unit, gateway, auto-reply, agents, Codex, and extension shards, including all 86 loopback MCP tests in their owning gateway-server shard;
- exact-head proof passed 14 selected assertions across 18 suites with zero failures;
- exact-head Codex lifecycle, binding, and login-profile compatibility passed 215 tests;
- focused CLI preparation tests confirm trusted-internal policy is preserved while owner identity remains false;
- prior focused suites passed 173 compaction/overflow, 98 harness-selection, and 15 manual-compaction propagation tests;
- prompt snapshots are current;

target.title: fix(cron): persist startup catch-up deferrals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #102236. A startup overflow catch-up slot could be persisted to SQLite while its protection marker existed only in memory. Restarting again before that slot fired let maintenance advance the job to its next natural cron slot, silently losing the deferred run.

## Why This Change Was Made

The deferral marker now lives on `CronJobState` as `pendingCatchupDeferral`, so the existing `state_json` persistence and rollback paths own the slot and marker together. The process-local Set and its parallel rollback bookkeeping are removed. Maintenance clears the persisted marker when the slot arrives, when no valid deferred slot remains, or when the job is disabled; execution also clears it after an outcome. Existing rows need no migration because an absent field means no pending deferral.

## User Impact

Overflow system-event cron jobs keep their staggered startup catch-up run across repeated gateway restarts instead of silently skipping to the next natural schedule. Unrelated stale future cron slots are still repaired normally.

## Evidence

- Real SQLite restart path: one service starts and persists an overflow deferral, a fresh service starts 3 seconds later against the same store, the original 5-second slot survives, executes once, and clears its marker.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two operator visibility gaps in OpenClaw security posture checks:

1. **`plugins.load.paths` trust-boundary risk** — Operators can point `plugins.load.paths` at arbitrary local directories, but `openclaw security audit` did not evaluate those configured paths for filesystem risk (world-writable paths, missing entries, bundled aliases, synced folders) before runtime plugin load.

target.title: fix(browser): normalize geolocation permission origins
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users calling Browser `/set/geolocation` with a normal page URL in `origin`, such as `https://x.test/path`, did not get the same origin normalization as `/permissions/grant`, and malformed or `file://` origins were not rejected before the Playwright geolocation set path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Browser routes now share one HTTP(S) origin parser. `/set/geolocation` normalizes supplied origins to `URL.origin` before invoking Playwright and rejects non-HTTP(S) or malformed origins for geolocation set operations with the same error used by the dedicated permissions route.

The clear path intentionally returns before parsing `origin`, because clearing geolocation and permissions does not use an origin. This preserves existing clients that send stale or malformed origin fields while clearing state.

## User Impact

Users can pass page URLs as geolocation permission origins and get the expected site origin grant. Invalid local-file or malformed origins fail fast with a clear 400 response for set operations instead of reaching the browser mutation path. `clear=true` still clears geolocation even when an unused origin field is malformed.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(line): cap user profile cache
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an unbounded in-process `userProfileCache` in the LINE send path (`extensions/line/src/send.ts`). Profile lookups are cached for 5 minutes (TTL) but had no entry-count cap, so gateways serving many distinct LINE users accumulate Map entries indefinitely until process restart.

**Concrete scenario:** A LINE gateway processing inbound messages from 10 000 distinct users over several hours caches each `getUserProfile` result. With no size cap, the cache grows without bound.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a 1 024-entry cap via the existing `pruneMapToMaxSize` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/collection-runtime`, matching Slack / Discord / Nextcloud Talk channel caches.

`touchLineUserProfileCache` deletes + sets so Map insertion order refreshes on both write and TTL-valid read hits (same LRU-on-access pattern as `extensions/slack/src/channel-type.ts`). Active users stay under the cap; idle oldest-inserted entries evict first.

No config/env knobs. TTL behavior is unchanged.

## User Impact

**Before:** Long-lived LINE gateways accumulate one `userProfileCache` entry per distinct user indefinitely.

**After:** Cache stays at ≤ 1 024 entries. Recently touched profiles survive eviction; untouched oldest entries are pruned. First 1 024 distinct users behave as before until the cap is exceeded.

## Evidence

- `extensions/line/src/send.ts` — `LINE_USER_PROFILE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 1024`, `touchLineUserProfileCache` (delete + set + `pruneMapToMaxSize`) on write and TTL hit
- `extensions/line/src/monitor.ts` — inbound path calls `getUserDisplayName` → `getUserProfile`
- Sibling pattern: `extensions/slack/src/channel-type.ts` (`getCachedSlackConversationInfo` / `setCachedSlackConversationInfo`)
- Shared helper: `src/infra/map-size.ts` (`pruneMapToMaxSize`)
- Regression: `extensions/line/src/send.test.ts`
  - eviction past cap via `getUserDisplayName`
  - recently touched entry retained under cap

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** LINE user-profile Map no longer grows without bound; active entries refresh insertion order so they survive pruning.
- **Canonical reachability path:**

```text
LINE inbound webhook (monitor)
  → getUserDisplayName(userId)
  → getUserProfile(userId)
  → touchLineUserProfileCache (delete + set)
  → pruneMapToMaxSize(userProfileCache, 1024)
```

- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; production `getUserDisplayName` / `getUserProfile` through the real unmocked `pruneMapToMaxSize` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/collection-runtime`. Only the LINE Messaging API `getProfile` client is stubbed (no live LINE credentials in this environment).
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Cap and LRU-on-access match Slack conversation-info and other channel `pruneMapToMaxSize` caches. No new config/env surface.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS Darwin 24.3.0 arm64, Node v22.22.0, pnpm 11.2.2, branch `fix/line-cap-user-profile-cache` rebased onto `upstream/main` (head `ecf8259c0af14fd5b5ae6e4db0b4b1275b71a99d`).
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/line/src/send.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ |extension-line| extensions/line/src/send.test.ts > LINE send helpers > caches profile results by default 0ms
 ✓ |extension-line| extensions/line/src/send.test.ts > LINE send helpers > evicts oldest profile cache entries once the cache exceeds its cap 6ms
 ✓ |extension-line| extensions/line/src/send.test.ts > LINE send helpers > keeps recently touched profile entries under the cache cap 6ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 6.68s
```

Regression flow (caller path `getUserDisplayName`):

1. Resolve `U-first` → 1 API call, cached
2. Resolve `U-fill-1` … `U-fill-1024` → 1 024 more API calls; `U-first` evicted at cap
3. Resolve `U-first` again → 1 API call (eviction proven)

LRU retention flow:

1. Fill cache to 1 024 including `U-keep`
2. Touch `U-keep` (0 extra API calls; insertion order refreshed)
3. Insert `U-new` → oldest untouched (`U-fill-1`) evicted; `U-keep` still cached (0 API calls)

target.title: fix(msteams): add timeouts to file consent upload requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Teams file consent uploads validated the SharePoint consent URL, then performed the upload PUT without a request deadline. If the upload request never completed, the accepted file delivery path could remain pending indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a bounded consent upload timeout using the existing timer timeout resolver, and keep the abort timer active until the upload request finishes. The upload deadline is transfer-aware: it keeps a 5 minute base stall bound, then adds size-derived transfer budget so valid large SharePoint uploads are not cut off by a fixed 5 minute ceiling. The SSRF host/IP validation and upload headers/body semantics are unchanged.

## User Impact

When a Teams file consent upload stalls, OpenClaw now aborts the request instead of waiting forever, so the file delivery flow can fail quickly and surface the error path. Large valid file-consent uploads get additional budget based on payload size instead of sharing the same fixed deadline as a small upload.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.test.ts` passed: 68 tests.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.test.ts` passed.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.test.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Transfer-aware proof: `resolveMSTeamsSharePointUploadTimeoutMs(100 * 1024 * 1024)` now resolves to 700000ms: 300000ms base plus 400000ms transfer budget at 256KiB/s.
- Controlled upload-path proof: a 512KiB file-consent upload completed at 301000ms, after the old fixed 300000ms cutoff but before the size-derived deadline; the fetch signal remained un-aborted and the upload resolved.
- Exact-head local HTTPS transport proof at `3702e4702fe54c8662f3536cf299399cfe2d5ade`: `uploadToConsentUrl` performed real HTTPS `PUT` requests against a loopback stalled/slow-success server. The harness used a self-signed certificate with `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` and a test validation override for the `127.0.0.1` allowlist/DNS so the local server could stand in for a Teams/SharePoint upload URL; the production upload path still validated HTTPS and sent the real request body, headers, and abort signal.


target.title: feat(ui): name Control UI sessions created with /new
target.body:
Closes #93422

## What Problem This Solves

Control UI intercepts typed `/new` commands, but it currently discards trailing text when creating a fresh dashboard session. Users who type `/new Research Plan` therefore get another UUID-like session entry instead of a session they can identify in the sidebar.

## Why This Change Was Made

Control UI now forwards the trimmed text after `/new` through its existing chat-pane adapter as the already-supported `sessions.create` `label`. Bare `/new` keeps its current behavior, `/name <title>` remains the command for renaming the current session, non-Control-UI `/new <model>` behavior is unchanged, and the existing `session.dmScope: "main"` reset-in-place path is not changed.

This stays entirely within the existing label contract: no Gateway protocol, schema, persistence, migration, permission, model-routing, or cross-channel command changes are included.

## User Impact

When `/new Research Plan` creates a new Control UI dashboard session, users immediately switch to a session shown as `Research Plan` in the session list. Users can still rename that session later with `/name <title>`.

## Evidence

- Real Control UI proof against an isolated local Gateway: typed `/new Research Plan`, observed the UI switch to a new dashboard session, and saw `Research Plan` appear in the sidebar. A follow-up `sessions.list` returned the same dashboard key with both `label` and `displayName` set to `Research Plan`. Before/after screenshots were captured for the review handoff.
- Full affected UI test files: 203 tests passed across `chat-send.test.ts` and `chat-pane.test.ts`.
- `pnpm tsgo:test:ui` passed.
- Changed TypeScript files passed oxlint.
- All six changed files passed `oxfmt --check`.
- `pnpm docs:list` passed with the updated slash-command documentation.

target.title: fix(feishu): bound stalled docx image URL reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users rendering or uploading Feishu docx images from remote URLs could have the docx workflow hang when the remote image response body stalled.

## Why This Change Was Made

Docx image URL reads now go through a Feishu-local remote image reader that applies the selected account's Feishu HTTP timeout as two targeted deadlines: a response-header deadline and a response-body idle deadline. It no longer uses the setting as a complete-operation download deadline, so healthy large image transfers that keep making progress are not cut off solely because total elapsed time exceeds the header timeout. File upload remote reads keep their existing behavior, so this stays scoped to docx image handling.

## User Impact

Feishu docx image processing now degrades through the existing error handling instead of blocking the whole document operation on a stalled remote image body. Account-specific Feishu timeout settings are honored for docx image response headers and stalled body reads without changing the Feishu config schema.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/docx.test.ts` passed: 20 tests.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/feishu/src/docx.ts extensions/feishu/src/docx.test.ts` passed.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/feishu/src/docx.ts extensions/feishu/src/docx.test.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Selected-account timeout proof: `feishu_doc` write with `resolveFeishuToolAccount(...).config.httpTimeoutMs = 1234` now calls `readRemoteMediaBuffer` with `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 1234` and `readIdleTimeoutMs: 1234` for the markdown image URL.
- Exact-head local media runtime proof at `28db697a9e527f82a196c7370fb1774691551f85`: the shared media reader was run against a local HTTP image server with the same deadline shape used by the Feishu docx image path. The body-stall case sent response headers and left the body open, then failed through `MediaFetchError`; the slow-progress case used `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 60` and kept sending chunks for 529ms, proving there is no complete-operation deadline cutting off a healthy transfer that continues to make progress.

Command:

```text
node --import tsx --input-type=module - <<'JS'
# local HTTP image server + readRemoteMediaBuffer({ responseHeaderTimeoutMs, readIdleTimeoutMs }) harness
JS
```

target.title: fix(security): keep secret mask from splitting UTF-16 surrogate pairs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where masking a credential-like value that contains astral characters (e.g., emoji) could produce isolated UTF-16 surrogate halves at the head or tail of the masked preview.

## Why This Change Was Made

`maskApiKey` sliced its prefix/suffix with raw `String.prototype.slice`, which can bisect surrogate pairs. It now uses the repository's existing `sliceUtf16Safe` helper so the visible prefix and suffix always fall on safe UTF-16 boundaries. The change is scoped to the secret mask function and its existing test.

## User Impact

Credential previews shown in setup prompts and status output remain readable and well-formed when the underlying value contains non-BMP characters.

## Evidence

- Added regression tests in `src/security/secret-mask.test.ts` that assert no lone surrogates are emitted for short and long astral inputs.
- Existing ASCII masking cases remain unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Before the patch, `maskApiKey("😀")` returned `"\ud83d...\ude00"` (two isolated surrogate halves). After the patch it returns `"..."`, and `maskApiKey("😀abcdefghijklmno😀")` still returns `"😀abcdef...jklmno😀"`.
- **Real environment tested:** Local checkout of `fix/secret-mask-utf16-boundaries` at `a6df5a1bd419cc9da7ddeca214de3e7c2ae3223a`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  node --import tsx -e 'import { maskApiKey } from "./src/security/secret-mask.ts"; for (const v of ["😀", "😀abcdefghijklmno😀", "1234567890abcdefghijklmnop"]) console.log(JSON.stringify(maskApiKey(v)));'
  ```
  And to verify the masked astral value survives a real disk round-trip without corrupting:
  ```bash
  node --import tsx -e 'import { maskApiKey } from "./src/security/secret-mask.ts"; import { writeFileSync, readFileSync, mkdtempSync } from "node:fs"; import { tmpdir } from "node:os"; import { join } from "node:path"; const f = join(mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "sm-")), "m.txt"); const m = maskApiKey("😀abcdefghijklmno😀"); writeFileSync(f, m, "utf8"); const r = readFileSync(f, "utf8"); console.log(JSON.stringify(r)); console.log("round-trip ok:", r === m);'
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```
  "..."
  "😀abcdef...jklmno😀"
  "12345678...ijklmnop"

  "😀abcdef...jklmno😀"
  round-trip ok: true
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** The regression test `does not split UTF-16 surrogate pairs at mask boundaries` passes, `encodeURIComponent(masked)` does not throw, and the masked value survives a disk write/read round-trip without corrupting astral characters.
- **What was not tested:** No runtime provider/channel integration; change is a pure string-formatting helper.

_AI-assisted PR: changes and tests were generated with AI assistance and manually reviewed._

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Workboard claim authorization compared claim tokens with ordinary string equality. Claim tokens are redacted credentials that let a worker other than the recorded owner heartbeat, release, or mutate a claimed card, so their validation should use the same timing-safe primitive as other OpenClaw secret-bearing authorization surfaces.

## Why This Change Was Made

Routes all four Workboard claim-token checks through the existing `safeEqualSecret` Plugin SDK contract while leaving owner-id comparisons and authorization behavior unchanged. This covers both tool-level preflight checks and store-level heartbeat, release, and mutation enforcement without adding configuration or dependencies.

## User Impact

Workboard claim authorization now avoids data-dependent string comparison timing for claim tokens. Existing valid and invalid token behavior, error messages, and card workflows remain unchanged.

target.title: fix(github-copilot): bound Copilot token exchange fetch timeout
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where GitHub Copilot API token exchange could hang forever after a cache miss when `api.<domain>/copilot_internal/v2/token` stopped responding.

`resolveCopilotApiToken()` in `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.ts` issued a bare `fetch` with no `AbortSignal` / timeout. Callers across model auth, embeddings, media understanding, and simple-completion refresh all reuse this helper, so a stalled exchange left those surfaces waiting indefinitely.

Sibling paths already had deadlines:

- GitHub Copilot device-code / token-poll OAuth uses `AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)`
- Copilot embedding `/models` discovery timeout is covered by open PR #102886

This PR covers the remaining exchange path itself.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a fixed internal 30-second per-request deadline via `AbortSignal.timeout` on the Copilot token-exchange fetch, aligned with `COPILOT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` in the Copilot OAuth helper. Map `AbortError` / `TimeoutError` to:

`Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms`

Preserve the original abort cause with `{ cause: error }`. The published `resolveCopilotApiToken` signature is unchanged — no public `timeoutMs` override.

## User Impact

**Before:** After Copilot token cache miss/expiry, a hung GitHub token-exchange endpoint could block Copilot model/embedding/auth refresh forever.

**After:** The exchange aborts at 30s with an explicit timeout error instead of hanging.

## Evidence

- `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.ts` — fixed internal `AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)` on `resolveCopilotApiToken` exchange fetch; timeout errors preserve `{ cause }`
- Regression: `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.test.ts`
  - success path asserts the exchange request carries an `AbortSignal`
  - hung mocked fetch aborts with the 30s timeout message
  - real `node:http` loopback that accepts TCP but never writes headers aborts via transport `fetchImpl` race (~250ms) while production still installs the 30s signal

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Copilot token exchange no longer leaves the GitHub `copilot_internal/v2/token` HTTP request unbounded when the remote endpoint stops responding before headers return.
- **Canonical reachability path:**

```text
cache miss / expired github-copilot.token.json
  → resolveCopilotApiToken (plugin-sdk/provider-auth)
  → GET api.<domain>/copilot_internal/v2/token
  → AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)
  → TimeoutError → "Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms"
```

Callers that hit this helper include `extensions/github-copilot` token/models/embeddings paths, `src/agents/simple-completion-runtime.ts`, and `src/media-understanding/image.ts`.

- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; production `resolveCopilotApiToken` exercised against a real Node HTTP server that accepts the connection and never sends response bytes (no live GitHub credential / blackhole required).
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Timeout value matches sibling Copilot OAuth request timeout (`30_000`). Published Plugin SDK signature unchanged (no `timeoutMs` param). Does not change device-code login or embedding `/models` discovery (the latter is #102886).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (Darwin), Node v22.22.0, branch `fix/copilot-token-exchange-timeout`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.test.ts -t "aborts hung Copilot token exchange|plus-signed Copilot token" --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ accepts plus-signed Copilot token expiry strings 860ms
 ✓ aborts hung Copilot token exchange instead of waiting forever 1018ms
 ✓ aborts hung Copilot token exchange over HTTP transport 797ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed | 19 skipped (22)
 Duration  23.07s
```

- **Observed result after fix:**
  - Happy-path exchange request includes an `AbortSignal`
  - Mock hung fetch rejects with `Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms`
  - Real loopback hang (TCP accept, no headers) rejects with `Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms` in ~797ms wall time, proving undici/`fetch` honors abort on a live socket while the published helper keeps the fixed 30s deadline
- **What was not tested:** Live `api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token` blackhole with a real GitHub OAuth token; post-header body stalls after headers return.

target.title: fix(googlechat): bound webhook cert fetch during token verification
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Google Chat webhook authentication could hang indefinitely when Google's signing-certificate endpoint accepts a connection but never completes the HTTP response.

This path runs on cold start and again every 10 minutes when the cert cache expires, so a stalled `googleapis.com` request blocks all incoming Google Chat message verification until the gateway process is restarted.

Outbound Google Chat API timeouts were already addressed in #102227; this PR closes the remaining unbounded fetch in the inbound auth path. Related but distinct from #103627, which bounds the shared Gaxios Google-auth transport rather than this direct webhook certificate fetch.

Related: #5126

## Why This Change Was Made

`fetchChatCerts()` in `extensions/googlechat/src/auth.ts` called `fetchWithSsrFGuard` without a deadline. The fix adds a 30-second `timeoutMs` via a local `GOOGLECHAT_AUTH_TIMEOUT_MS` constant, matching the deadline already used for outbound Chat API calls and sibling channel auth paths.

No config/env knobs were added. The shared Gaxios transport timeout remains separate complementary work (#103627).

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled cert endpoint leaves webhook auth pending forever; incoming Google Chat messages fail silently with no timeout error and no lane release.

**After:** Cert fetch aborts after 30 seconds with a concrete error; verification returns `{ ok: false, reason: ... }` and the gateway can continue processing other traffic.

## Evidence

- `extensions/googlechat/src/auth.ts` — `GOOGLECHAT_AUTH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000` passed as `timeoutMs` to `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in `fetchChatCerts()`
- Regression: `extensions/googlechat/src/auth.test.ts`
  - asserts exact `timeoutMs: 30_000` on the guarded cert fetch
  - surfaces `{ ok: false, reason: /aborted/i }` when the guard rejects with `AbortError`
- Target-level assertion updated in `extensions/googlechat/src/targets.test.ts`

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Direct Google Chat webhook certificate retrieval no longer waits forever when the cert endpoint accepts TCP but never returns response bytes.
- **Canonical reachability path:**

```text
inbound Google Chat webhook (project-number audience)
  → verifyGoogleChatRequest
  → fetchChatCerts
  → fetchWithSsrFGuard({ url: CHAT_CERTS_URL, timeoutMs: 30_000 })
  → buildTimeoutAbortSignal deadline aborts stalled request
  → { ok: false, reason: ... }
```

- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; production `verifyGoogleChatRequest` → `fetchChatCerts` through the real unmocked `fetchWithSsrFGuard` against a controlled hanging `node:http` loopback. The `googleapis.com` cert URL keeps the real SSRF hostname allowlist satisfied; only `globalThis.fetch` is redirected onto the loopback origin so the guard's composed timeout signal rides the real request.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Deadline matches outbound Google Chat API timeout and sibling auth control-plane paths (30s). Does not change Gaxios Google-auth transport (#103627) or outbound Chat control/media (#102227).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (darwin), Node via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs`, branch `fix/googlechat-api-request-timeout`, exact head after squash/rebase onto `upstream/main`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/auth.proof.test.ts extensions/googlechat/src/auth.test.ts --reporter=verbose
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/targets.test.ts -t "verifyGoogleChatRequest" --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ googlechat cert-fetch — real guard proof > times out a stalled cert fetch through the real production guard 523ms
 ✓ Google Chat cert-fetch timeout > passes timeoutMs to fetchWithSsrFGuard when fetching certs 0ms
 ✓ Google Chat cert-fetch timeout > surfaces an abort error when the cert endpoint stalls 0ms

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  3 passed (3)

 ✓ verifyGoogleChatRequest > fetches Chat certs through the guarded fetch for project-number tokens
 … (10 verifyGoogleChatRequest tests passed)
```

Proof details (real guard, real loopback, production deadline fired after receipt):

- Real `fetchWithSsrFGuard` schedules the production 30s deadline via `buildTimeoutAbortSignal`
- Loopback server confirms the cert request arrived and never responds
- Mutation control: without firing the deadline, verification stays `pending` past 500ms
- Firing the captured production deadline aborts the in-flight request; `verifyGoogleChatRequest` returns `{ ok: false, reason: /aborted|timed out|timeout/i }`
- JWT verification is never reached (`verifySignedJwtWithCertsAsync` not called)

target.title: feat: add WhatsApp phone-code login
target.body:
Closes #85867

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users connecting WhatsApp from a headless, remote, or QR-unavailable environment had no first-class alternative to scanning a QR code.

It also fixes a retry edge case where an interrupted phone-code attempt could leave partial Baileys credentials on disk. Those incomplete credentials could be mistaken for a linked account and prevent a clean QR or phone-code retry.

## Why This Change Was Made

WhatsApp now owns an interactive login choice inside its existing channel login callback, following the established plugin-local setup pattern. Running `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp` prompts the user to either scan a QR code or link with a phone number; QR remains the default choice.

The WhatsApp plugin owns phone-number validation, Baileys `requestPairingCode` handling, pairing-code display, socket restart behavior, and stale partial-credential cleanup. The cleanup reuses the existing credential-save queue and logout ownership checks so it cannot race a completed pairing save or delete an unmanaged auth directory.

Baileys `7.0.0-rc13` derives linked-device metadata differently across its QR and phone-code pairing paths. [During QR registration](https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/blob/8053b086ecc97ec3f78299561de11959bab05d39/src/Utils/validate-connection.ts#L84-L105), OpenClaw's existing `"cli"` client name falls back to the Chrome platform type while preserving `"openclaw"` as the device name, producing the observed `Google Chrome (openclaw)` label. [Phone-code pairing maps the browser name separately](https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/blob/8053b086ecc97ec3f78299561de11959bab05d39/src/Utils/companion-reg-client-utils.ts#L16-L34) and [sends its companion platform type and display metadata directly](https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/blob/8053b086ecc97ec3f78299561de11959bab05d39/src/Socket/socket.ts#L758-L808), so the same `"cli"` tuple would not carry the Chrome identity.

Rather than introduce a phone-code-only browser override, every WhatsApp socket now uses the canonical `["openclaw", "Chrome", VERSION]` tuple. This keeps one socket-identity definition across QR, phone-code pairing, startup, and reconnect. Based on the metadata Baileys sends, both pairing methods are expected to appear as `Google Chrome (openclaw)`; physical-device verification remains outstanding.

This normalization does not re-pair or rename existing linked accounts. With saved credentials, Baileys uses its authenticated login path; under OpenClaw's current socket settings, the old `"cli"` and new `"Chrome"` tuples produce a byte-identical login payload. Normal startup and reconnect continue using the established session credentials.

This PR adds no production core CLI, channel-login, or Plugin SDK contract.

## User Impact

Users can link WhatsApp in either of two ways from the same command:

- **Scan QR code** — the existing default flow.
- **Link with phone number** — enter a number with country code, then enter the generated pairing code in WhatsApp under **Linked Devices → Link with phone number**.

Both methods are expected to create the same `Google Chrome (openclaw)` Linked Devices identity. Existing linked sessions, account selection through `--account`, and normal send/receive/status behavior remain on the existing WhatsApp session path.

If phone-code pairing is interrupted, OpenClaw no longer reports the partial credentials as linked. A later QR or phone-code login can safely clear managed stale state and retry.

## Evidence

Validated on exact head `336aa3f33c0ed427250d43fae60e8d82dbb2cf12`:

- Focused CLI and WhatsApp Testbox proof: **155 tests passed** on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kx96g5keh29qervsrk57kzq2`.
- Full changed-surface gate passed on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kx98stb6n0rpjfffx3x2ccev`:
  - `pnpm check:changed`
- Full production build passed on the same Testbox:
  - `pnpm build`
- Whitespace validation passed:
  - `git diff --check`
- GitHub CI completed with no failing or pending relevant checks.
- A read-only master quality gate reconciled all 23 changed paths, found the implementation scope-fit, and reported no code findings.

Remaining proof gap: this exact head has not been exercised against a physical WhatsApp device. Before merge, live verification should cover phone-number pairing and its native restart, QR login, an existing linked session, and the `Google Chrome (openclaw)` Linked Devices label.

target.title: fix(qqbot): guard mentionPatterns against ReDoS via compileSafeRegex
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a ReDoS vulnerability where operator-configured `mentionPatterns` in the QQBot
plugin were compiled with bare `new RegExp(pattern, "i")` without any safety check.
A pattern containing nested repetition such as `(a+)+$` compiles successfully but
causes catastrophic backtracking when matched against attacker-controlled message
content, pushing CPU to 100% and making the gateway unresponsive.

Attack chain: set `mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$"]` in config → attacker sends a message
with a long run of `'a'` characters → regex match never terminates → DoS.

The same class of bug was previously fixed in MCP glob patterns (#100330).
`compileSafeRegex` from `src/security/safe-regex.ts` is already exposed through
`openclaw/plugin-sdk/security-runtime` for exactly this use.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace `new RegExp(pattern, "i")` with `compileSafeRegex(pattern, "i")`. The helper
rejects patterns with nested repetition and returns `null` for both unsafe and invalid
patterns, so the loop simply skips them — same observable behavior as before for valid
safe patterns, silent rejection for dangerous ones.

## User Impact

**Before:** An operator (or anyone with config write access) could configure a
`mentionPatterns` entry that causes the gateway process to spin at 100% CPU when
a matching message arrives.

**After:** Patterns with nested repetition are rejected at match time and skipped.
Safe patterns continue to work normally.

## Evidence

Node: v22.22.0 — macOS Darwin 24.3.0 arm64

**LOC** — `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/group/mention.ts`: +4/−5 (import + replace).
`extensions/qqbot/src/engine/group/mention.test.ts`: +20 (2 new regression cases).

**Before — catastrophic backtracking via raw `new RegExp`:**

```
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(20)+"b") →   65.5 ms
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(24)+"b") →  156.9 ms
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(26)+"b") →  640.7 ms
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(28)+"b") → 2522.4 ms  (2.5 s — gateway stalls)
```

Each +2 characters roughly 4× the time (exponential growth). At 64 characters the gateway
process would be unresponsive for minutes.

**After — `compileSafeRegex` guard, constant-time rejection:**

```
compileSafeRegex("(a+)+$", "i") → null (rejected before RegExp construction)
detectWasMentioned({ content: "a".repeat(24)+"b", mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$"] }) → false (0.065 ms)
detectWasMentioned({ content: "a".repeat(28)+"b", mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$"] }) → false (0.003 ms)
```

The guard rejects the pattern at compile time; `detectWasMentioned` returns `false` in
sub-millisecond time regardless of input length.

**Safe pattern still matches after a rejected unsafe one:**

```
detectWasMentioned({
  content: "hello @bot",
  mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$", "@bot"],
}) → true (0.130 ms)
```

**Regression tests — 24/24:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qqbot/src/engine/group/mention.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 ✓ detectWasMentioned > rejects ReDoS patterns via compileSafeRegex guard    0ms
 ✓ detectWasMentioned > still matches safe patterns after a rejected unsafe one  0ms
 ✓ detectWasMentioned > ignores invalid regex patterns gracefully  0ms
 ... (21 more)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  24 passed (24)
   Duration  370ms
```

`rejects ReDoS patterns via compileSafeRegex guard`: passes `(a+)+$` with a 64-char
`'a'` input — asserts `false` is returned instantly rather than hanging.

`still matches safe patterns after a rejected unsafe one`: confirms the unsafe pattern
is skipped and the next safe pattern still matches.

What was not tested: live QQBot message delivery with a real QQ group.
Crabbox/Testbox remote CI was not run at submission time.

Related: #100330 (MCP glob ReDoS — same fix pattern)

target.title: Fix/OpenAI device code request timeout
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running OpenAI Codex device-code login (`openclaw models auth login --provider openai --device-code`, or the equivalent configure/wizard auth choice) could hang forever when a single `auth.openai.com` HTTP request stopped responding.

Before this patch, the flow only enforced a 15-minute poll-loop deadline around authorization waiting. The three `fetch` calls for user-code request, authorization poll, and token exchange had no per-request `AbortSignal` timeout, so a stalled TCP/proxy/blackhole response could bypass that deadline and leave the CLI spinner stuck. A server that returned headers and then stalled the body could also escape an incomplete timeout catch.

## Why This Change Was Made

Treat each device-code HTTP call as one timed operation: headers fetch plus bounded body read under the same `AbortSignal.timeout` (30s, aligned with the sibling ChatGPT browser OAuth token request timeout). Poll requests clamp that timeout to the remaining 15-minute authorization deadline and retry on per-operation timeout (including post-header body stalls) until the overall deadline expires. User-code and token-exchange timeouts fail fast with a clear error.

Scope stays OpenAI Codex device-code login HTTP only; browser OAuth and other providers are unchanged.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hung device-code HTTP request (or a post-header body stall) could block `models auth login --device-code` indefinitely, even past the advertised 15-minute authorization window.

**After:** Each device-code request+body read aborts after 30 seconds (or sooner near the overall deadline). Poll timeouts retry within the 15-minute window; user-code and token-exchange stalls surface an explicit timeout error instead of hanging forever.

## Evidence

- `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.ts` — one operation deadline for fetch + body read on user-code, poll, and token-exchange; poll retries on timeout within the 15-minute deadline
- Regression: `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.test.ts`
  - hung user-code aborts with timeout error
  - poll retries after `TimeoutError` and completes
  - hung token exchange aborts with timeout error
  - success path asserts all three fetches carry an `AbortSignal`
  - real `node:http` partial-body stall: user-code / token-exchange abort with formatted timeout; poll retries and succeeds

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** OpenAI Codex device-code login no longer leaves individual HTTP operations unbounded when the remote endpoint stops responding before headers return, or returns headers and then stalls the body.
- **Canonical reachability path:** Operator runs device-code auth → `loginOpenAICodexDeviceCode` → `requestOpenAICodexDeviceCode` / `pollOpenAICodexDeviceCode` / `exchangeOpenAICodexDeviceCode` → `runOpenAICodexDeviceCodeRequest` (`fetch` + `readOpenAICodexDeviceBody` under `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`).
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; production device-code helpers exercised via colocated Vitest against a real hanging `node:http` loopback that sends headers then a partial JSON prefix and never finishes the body. Only `AbortSignal.timeout` duration is shortened for deterministic proof; the production fetch+body composition and error/retry mapping stay unmocked.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Matches the existing 30s OpenAI ChatGPT OAuth token request timeout; uses `AbortSignal.timeout` like GitHub Copilot device-flow request timeouts. Does not migrate this path onto `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in this change.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS, Node 22, product checkout on branch `fix/openai-device-code-request-timeout`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```
 ✓ aborts hung user-code requests instead of waiting forever 1ms
 ✓ retries device authorization polls after a per-request timeout 0ms
 ✓ aborts hung token exchange requests instead of waiting forever 0ms
 ✓ aborts when user-code headers arrive but the body never completes 31ms
 ✓ retries authorization polls after a post-header body stall 43ms
 ✓ aborts when token-exchange headers arrive but the body never completes 43ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
 Duration  1.37s
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 3.53s
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Hung user-code and token-exchange fetches abort with `OpenAI device code ... timed out after 30000ms`; a poll `TimeoutError` (including post-header body stall) is retried and the login can still succeed within the overall deadline. Real loopback partial-body stalls exercise production body consumption under the same operation signal.
- **What was not tested:** Live `openclaw models auth login --provider openai --device-code` against a real stalled `auth.openai.com` endpoint.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix.

target.title: fix(core): make indexed access explicit across remaining src (NUIA phase 3b)
target.body:
Related: #104600

## What Problem This Solves

Phase 3b of the `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adoption (#104600): the remaining 669 unchecked-index errors across all of `src/**` outside `src/agents` — auto-reply, infra, config, cli, gateway, commands, security, and 20 smaller directories. With this landed, the entire core program (src + packages) is index-safe and ready for the flag flip in phase 3c.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pure burn-down to zero (repo probe 669 → 0), 234 files, eight commits (including mid-flight rebases across the sqlite-sessions flip and the pre-2026.4 shim removal, whose new code was made index-safe here too). The fix ladder from prior phases applied: iteration over indexing, boundary guards on genuinely-optional input, named invariants (`expectDefined`), closed-key tightening.

This chunk needed real review pressure, documented here honestly:
- The first pass mass-produced 416 `expectDefined(..., "indexed value")` escape hatches; a rework round eliminated every generic context (72 restructured away, 65 converted to real guards, the rest given site-specific contexts) and removed introduced casts/assertions.
- Per-commit structured reviews then caught **five genuine absence-is-legitimate bugs** the pattern had created, each now fixed and test-covered: CLI `--profile`/route-args missing next tokens must take their existing miss paths (the "rejects missing profile value" test proves absence is input, not invariant); nested `help X Y --help` normalization must compare against the last positional; first-time plugin install must tolerate an absent `cfg.plugins`; dependency-denylist scanning must skip omitted manifest dependency sections (the guard was one line below the throw); status-scan must pass its optional params through unchanged.
- One SDK-boundary lesson: an early fix made `getChatChannelMeta` honestly optional, which would have changed a shipped plugin-SDK signature (two bundled extensions consume it). Final shape preserves the SDK contract (defined for bundled ids, fail-loud on impossible misses) and adds `findChatChannelMeta` for the drift-tolerant core paths — reviewed clean (0.98).
- Root-cause fixes preferred over wrappers: the tailnet resolver now guarantees `string` at the source (guarded first-IP) instead of a caller-side undefined-throw; `PROVIDER_LABELS` became a `satisfies`-typed closed record (static reads provably defined, dynamic lookups through an honest `string | undefined` helper), deleting ~10 assertions.
- Sensitive-area equivalence: security parsers remain fail-closed; gateway event/byte ordering untouched; SQLite query shapes unchanged; config migration behavior identical.

## User Impact

No behavior change on healthy paths. Plugin install, CLI parsing, and status scanning behave identically including their absence paths (now proven by types instead of convention).

## Evidence

- NUIA probe: repo 669 → 0 under the core lane; fresh non-incremental core, core-test, ui, and scripts lanes all 0 errors.
- Blacksmith Testbox: full `pnpm check` + `pnpm check:test-types` green on the final tree; across seven battery runs every completed test file passed (thousands; the only real failures were the seven bugs fixed above), with all aborts being box-level worker/lease deaths under memory pressure — exact-head sharded CI on this PR is the complete-suite arbiter.
- Per-commit structured reviews: parts 1–3 reviewed individually (the two "incorrect" verdicts drove the fixes above); both correction commits reviewed clean (0.96 / 0.96).
- 173 tests across the three originally-failing CLI files now pass; plugins/status/infra suites green.

target.title: fix(discord): add timeout to guarded gateway metadata fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord HTTP calls through `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded` could hang indefinitely. `/gateway/bot` already had `withAbortTimeout`, but the shared guarded fetch used as the Discord REST `fetchImpl` had no `timeoutMs`, so a stalled Discord API connection could block gateway metadata/REST work forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass an explicit `timeoutMs` into `fetchWithSsrFGuard` from `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded`, defaulting to the existing 30s Discord gateway-info timeout, and thread the resolved `gatewayInfoTimeoutMs` from `createDiscordGatewayPlugin` into that fetchImpl (including proxy and invalid-proxy fallback paths).

## User Impact

Discord gateway metadata/REST fetches fail within the configured timeout instead of hanging when Discord's API stalls.

## Evidence

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-metadata.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-plugin.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text
 ✓ ... > returns under-cap response bodies and releases the guarded fetch
 ✓ ... > forwards a custom timeout to the guarded Discord metadata fetch
 ✓ ... > aborts when the shared guarded fetch times out before headers arrive 345ms
 ✓ ... > rejects oversized response body from a real loopback HTTP server
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  23 passed (23)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Guarded Discord gateway metadata/REST fetches now carry a request deadline.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `createDiscordGatewayPlugin` → `createDiscordGatewayMetadataFetch(..., gatewayInfoTimeoutMs)` → `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard({ timeoutMs })`.
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime HTTP; loopback Node server + real `fetchWithSsrFGuard` timeout path for the hang proof; production caller wiring asserted via mock expectations.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Reused existing `DEFAULT_DISCORD_GATEWAY_INFO_TIMEOUT_MS` / `resolveDiscordGatewayInfoTimeoutMs` and `fetchWithSsrFGuard` timeout contract; no new Discord config key.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS, Node via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`, loopback `node:http` server that accepts connections without writing headers.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-metadata.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-plugin.test.ts --reporter=verbose`
- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ |extension-discord| ... > forwards a custom timeout to the guarded Discord metadata fetch 1ms
 ✓ |extension-discord| ... > aborts when the shared guarded fetch times out before headers arrive 345ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  23 passed (23)
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Default guarded fetch passes `timeoutMs: 30_000`; custom option forwards; real guarded fetch aborts a stalled-header loopback request near 250ms.
- **What was not tested:** Live Discord API /gateway/bot against production Discord; full Gateway reconnect storm.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. Default remains the existing 30s gateway-info timeout, and operator `gatewayInfoTimeoutMs` / env override continue to apply through the same resolver.
